correctness.rationale: With R=b-C>0 the low digit obeys 1<=R+jd<=b-p-d-2<b, so s_j=1+R+jd=b-1-h_j. For any prime q|s_j the chosen m=1+tL gives b^m≡b mod q, trivially if q|b and by Fermat otherwise. Thus a common prime must divide b-1 and h_j, which divides H. The start increases with t. Every p terms represent all residue classes mod p and s_b(N)≡N mod p, proving the sharp obstruction. All primes of Q are odd and different from p, so CRT gives the stated density for the particular class (not necessarily the density of all admissible bases), and b-1=2^u p^a meets all conditions above C. Independently built the four full integers for b=41, d=4, p=5, m=991 and divided repeatedly by 41: sums 19,23,27,31 and gcds all 1. The frozen verify.py and recorded result report broader but finite examples only.

evidence: The broader theorem implies sharpness for every base in the frozen CRT class and every claimed prime-power subfamily member, after the displayed elementary inequalities and coprimality checks.

The larger span theorem is also independently recoverable by choosing R in [0,b-2] via CRT so 1+R+jd avoids primes of b-1. Each q|d forbids one R class; other q>=p forbid at most p-1. Then R+jd<=2b-1 and s_j=1+R+jd-e_j(b-1), with e_j in {0,1}. The earlier simultaneous exponent lemma gives term minus s_j congruent to (1+e_j)(b-1) modulo any prime of s_j; this is coprime to s_j because s_j is odd and coprime to b-1.
